extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in combinatorics/poset and lattice theory (advanced undergraduates/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, structural properties, and combinatorial constructions for partially ordered sets and lattices (posets, chains, ideals, products, semimodular/modular/distributive/geometric lattices, J(P), linear extensions, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Posets ordered by natural relations (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of posets built from common combinatorial objects: Bn (subsets of [n] ordered by inclusion), Dn (positive divisors of n ordered by divisibility), Πn (partitions of [n] ordered by refinement), Bn(q) (subspaces of Fn_q ordered by inclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These illustrate typical ways of producing posets from sets, divisibility, refinement, or subspace containment; used repeatedly as canonical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poset isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Two posets P and Q are isomorphic (P ∼= Q) if there exists an order-preserving bijection φ : P → Q whose inverse is order-preserving; equivalently s ≤ t in P iff φ(s) ≤ φ(t) in Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify posets that are the same up to relabeling; e.g., BS ∼= BT whenever #S = #T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak subposet vs induced subposet (subposet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak subposet: subset Q of elements of P with a partial ordering so that if s ≤ t in Q then s ≤ t in P. Induced subposet: subset Q of P with ordering inherited from P (i.e., s ≤ t in Q iff s ≤ t in P). 'Subposet' will mean induced subposet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite poset P has exactly 2^{#P} induced subposets. Distinguish weak subposet and induced subposet when comparing orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interval [s,t] and (s,t)
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed interval [s,t] := {u in P : s ≤ u ≤ t} (nonempty only when s ≤ t); open interval (s,t) := {u in P: s < u < t}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervals are used to define local finiteness and convexity; [s,s] = {s} and empty set not regarded as closed interval here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally finite poset
rubrics_metrics.description: A poset P is locally finite if every interval of P is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locally finite posets are determined by their cover relations and support Hasse diagram constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex subposet
rubrics_metrics.description: A subposet Q of P is convex if whenever s < t < u in P and s,u ∈ Q then t ∈ Q (equivalently Q is an interval-closed subset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convexity matters when restricting to intervals and when considering induced substructures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover relation and Hasse diagram
rubrics_metrics.description: t covers s (s ⋖ t) if s < t and there is no u with s < u < t; the Hasse diagram of a finite poset has vertices the elements and edges the cover relations, drawn so larger elements are above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hasse diagrams visually encode cover relations; a locally finite poset is determined by its cover relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjoining ˆ0 and ˆ1
rubrics_metrics.description: A poset P 'has a ˆ0' if there exists element ˆ0 in P with ˆ0 ≤ t for all t in P; similarly for ˆ1. One can adjoin a ˆ0 and/or ˆ1 to P to obtain a new poset with global minimum/maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjoining ˆ0/ˆ1 is a standard construction (see Figure 3.3); useful in lattice considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain, maximal chain, saturated chain
rubrics_metrics.description: A chain is a totally ordered subset of a poset. A chain C is maximal if it is not contained in a larger chain. C is saturated (or unreﬁnable) if there is no u ∉ C such that inserting u into C yields a chain (equivalently consecutive elements are covers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In locally finite posets saturated means each consecutive pair are covers; maximal implies saturated but not conversely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of a chain and rank / graded poset
rubrics_metrics.description: Length ℓ(C) of a finite chain C is #C − 1 (or other conventions); rank ℓ(P) := max{ℓ(C): C a chain}. P is graded of rank n if every maximal chain has the same length n; in that case there is a unique rank function ρ: P → {0,1,...,n} with ρ(minimal)=0 and ρ(t)=ρ(s)+1 when t covers s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank function gives levels; rank-generating function F(P,x)=Σ p_i x^i where p_i is number of elements of rank i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank-generating function
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graded poset P of rank n with p_i elements of rank i, define F(P,x)=Σ_{i=0}^n p_i x^i; for some infinite graded posets this becomes a power series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to record rank distribution; examples: F(Bn,x)=(1+x)^n, explicit formulas given for Dn, Πn, Bn(q) as q-analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multichain
rubrics_metrics.description: A multichain is a chain allowing repeated elements (a multiset whose underlying set is a chain); a multichain of length n can be regarded as t0 ≤ t1 ≤ ... ≤ tn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multichains are counted in later propositions and correspond to order-preserving maps into chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antichain (Sperner family)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset A of a poset P is an antichain if any two distinct elements of A are incomparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antichains correspond bijectively (for finite P) to order ideals via maximal elements of the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order ideal and dual order ideal (filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order ideal (down-set): I ⊆ P with s ∈ I and t ≤ s ⇒ t ∈ I. Dual order ideal (up-set / filter): I ⊆ P with s ∈ I and t ≥ s ⇒ t ∈ I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite P antichains A correspond to order ideals I (A = set of maximal elements of I); principal ideals Λ_t and principal dual ideals V_t defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: J(P): poset of order ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: J(P) denotes the set of all order ideals of P ordered by inclusion; J(P) is itself a poset (indeed a distributive lattice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J(P) will be investigated in detail; many combinatorial properties of P translate to properties of J(P).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations producing new posets: disjoint union and ordinal sum
rubrics_metrics.description: Disjoint union (direct sum) P + Q: union of disjoint posets P and Q with inherited orders. Ordinal sum P ⊕ Q: all elements of P are declared less than all elements of Q (besides internal orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to build connected posets; nP denotes disjoint union of P with itself n times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series-parallel posets
rubrics_metrics.description: Posets obtained from the one-element poset 1 by repeated disjoint union and ordinal sum are series-parallel; not all small posets are series-parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification/recognition exercises reference series-parallel property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct (cartesian) product of posets and rank-generating product formula
rubrics_metrics.description: P × Q ordered by (s,t) ≤ (s',t') iff s ≤ s' in P and t ≤ t' in Q. If P and Q are graded then F(P × Q, x) = F(P,x) F(Q,x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hasse diagram construction: replace each element of P by a copy of Q and connect according to cover relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinal product of posets and rank formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal product P ⊗ Q orders pairs with (s,t) ≤ (s',t') iff s < s' or (s = s' and t ≤ t'). If P and Q are graded and Q has rank r, then F(P ⊗ Q, x) = F(P, x^{r+1}) F(Q, x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinal product is not in general isomorphic to the direct product (gives different rank-generating function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual poset and self-duality
rubrics_metrics.description: Dual P* is poset on same set with order reversed: s ≤_{P*} t iff t ≤_P s. P is self-dual if P ∼= P*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duality preserves many properties; several small posets are self-dual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poset of order-preserving maps Q^P and cardinal arithmetic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: QP denotes set of order-preserving maps f : P → Q, given pointwise order f ≤ g if f(t) ≤ g(t) for all t. The usual cardinal-arithmetic-like rules (+ and × associative/commutative, distribution properties) hold for poset operations; various isomorphisms listed (e.g., (RP)Q ∼= R^{P}?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when reasoning about combinations of poset constructions and counting order-preserving maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lattice: existence of meets and joins
rubrics_metrics.description: A lattice is a poset L in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound (join s ∨ t) and greatest lower bound (meet s ∧ t); lattice operations satisfy associative, commutative, idempotent laws and absorption laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All finite lattices have a ˆ0 and ˆ1. Lattices can be defined axiomatically via ∨ and ∧ but the poset perspective is used here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet-semilattice / Join-semilattice and finite criterion for lattice (Prop 3.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A meet-semilattice (respectively join-) is a poset where every pair has a meet (respectively join). Proposition: a finite meet-semilattice with ˆ1 is a lattice (dually a finite join-semilattice with ˆ0 is a lattice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In finite case existence of one of the binary operations plus top/bottom suffices to ensure both exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete lattice
rubrics_metrics.description: A lattice where every subset has a meet and join; a complete lattice necessarily has ˆ0 and ˆ1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete lattices are important in order theory but many combinatorial lattices are finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semimodular (upper semimodular) lattice (Prop 3.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite lattice L is upper semimodular iff it is graded with rank function ρ satisfying ρ(s)+ρ(t) ≥ ρ(s ∧ t)+ρ(s ∨ t) for all s,t in L; equivalently, whenever s and t both cover s ∧ t, then s ∨ t covers both s and t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives both an algebraic (rank inequality) and a covering-pair combinatorial characterization; used to detect semimodularity and to prove modularity conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular lattice (characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite lattice L is modular iff it is graded and its rank function satisfies equality ρ(s)+ρ(t) = ρ(s ∧ t)+ρ(s ∨ t) for all s,t in L (equation (3.6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modularity can also be characterized by the identity (3.7): for all s,t,u with s ≤ u, (t ∨ s) ∧ u = t ∨ (s ∧ u).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complemented, relatively complemented, atomic, coatomic, uniquely complemented
rubrics_metrics.description: Complemented lattice with ˆ0,ˆ1: for every s there exists t with s ∧ t = ˆ0 and s ∨ t = ˆ1. If complements in an interval exist, lattice is relatively complemented. Atom: element covering ˆ0; atomic: every element is join of atoms. Coatom: element covered by ˆ1; coatomic similar. Uniquely complemented if each element's complement is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notions classify lattices (boolean algebras, geometric lattices, etc.) and link to matroid theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition linking semimodular, relatively complemented, atomic (Prop 3.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a finite semimodular lattice L, L is relatively complemented iff L is atomic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finite semimodular lattice satisfying either condition is called a finite geometric lattice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric lattices and relation to matroids
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite semimodular and atomic lattice is a geometric lattice. Geometric lattices arise from finite sets of points in affine or vector spaces where elements are intersections with subspaces; matroids are in bijection with geometric lattices whose atoms form the ground set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matroids abstract linearly independent sets; join of atoms rank equals cardinality of independent set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive lattice (definition via distributive laws (3.8))
rubrics_metrics.description: A lattice satisfying distributive laws (s ∨ (t ∧ u) = (s ∨ t) ∧ (s ∨ u) and dual) is distributive (and therefore modular). Examples: n, Bn, Dn are distributive while Πn (n≥3) and Bn(q) (n≥2) are not in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lattices J(P) of order ideals of any poset P are distributive; union and intersection correspond to ∨ and ∧.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem for Finite Distributive Lattices (FTFDL)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is a finite distributive lattice then there is a unique (up to isomorphism) poset P for which L ∼= J(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely J(P) determines P as subposet of join-irreducibles; this yields a bijection between posets of size n and distributive lattices of rank n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join-irreducible elements and correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: In a lattice, s is join-irreducible if s cannot be written as t ∨ u with t,s,u < s; in finite lattice equivalently s covers exactly one element. The join-irreducibles of J(P) correspond to elements of P (principal ideals Λ_s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 3.4.2: set of join-irreducibles of J(P) (as subposet) is isomorphic to P; used in proving FTFDL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitary distributive lattices and Jf(P) (Prop 3.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If every principal ideal of P is finite, then J_f(P) (finite order ideals of P) is a finitary distributive lattice; conversely, any finitary distributive lattice L arises as J_f(P) for P its join-irreducibles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends FTFDL to certain infinite locally finite distributive lattices where each principal ideal finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean algebra equivalences in finite distributive lattices
rubrics_metrics.description: In a finite distributive lattice L, the following are equivalent: (a) L is a boolean algebra; (b) L is complemented; (c) L is relatively complemented; (d) L is atomic; (e) ˆ1 is a join of atoms; (f) L is geometric; (g) every join-irreducible covers ˆ0; (h) if L has n join-irreducibles then |L| = 2^n; (i) rank-generating function is (1+x)^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalences characterize boolean algebras among distributive lattices (and link to Bn = J(n1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for drawing J(P) and computing F(J(P),x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithm: start with J(I) for minimal elements I of P (a boolean algebra), adjoin join-irreducibles for additional minimal elements one at a time, fill in joins of elements covering given ideals to form boolean algebras, and continue until J(P) is built; rank of I in J(P) equals |I|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated via step-by-step example (Figure 3.9) and used to compute rank-generating functions by hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting order-preserving maps, multichains and J(P^{m-1}) (Prop 3.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite poset P and m ∈ N, the following are equal: (a) number of order-preserving maps σ: P → [m]; (b) number of multichains 0̂ = I0 ≤ I1 ≤ ... ≤ Im = 1̂ of length m in J(P); (c) cardinality of J(P × [m−1]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit bijections described: maps correspond to chains of order ideals via preimages of initial segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjective order-preserving maps ↔ strict chains (Prop 3.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of surjective order-preserving maps σ: P → [m] equals number of chains 0̂ = I0 < I1 < ... < Im = 1̂ (strict chain of length m) in J(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define and count linear extensions when m = #P and σ bijective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear extension e(P) and relation to J(P)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear extension (topological sort) of P is an order-preserving bijection σ: P → [p]; the number e(P) of linear extensions equals number of maximal chains of J(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: e(P) is a primary measure of a poset's complexity; counting e(P) connects to lattice-path enumerations via embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding J(P) into Nk and polyhedral interpretation of e(P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition P into chains C1,...,Ck and define δ(I) = (#(I∩C1),...,#(I∩Ck)) giving an injective rank-preserving lattice homomorphism J(P) → Nk; Γ_δ = ⋃ conv(δ(T)) over boolean-intervals T is a compact polyhedral region; e(P) equals number of lattice paths in Γ_δ from δ(0̂) to δ(1̂) with unit coordinate steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies e(P) with counting lattice paths in a polyhedral region (connects to Catalan and binomial enumerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples linking poset classes to enumerative formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: If P = C1 + C2 (chains of sizes m,n) then e(P) = binomial(m+n,m). If P = 2×n (two chains of length n) then e(P) = Catalan number C_n (count of Dyck paths), and e(P) equals number of standard Young tableaux of rectangular shape 2×n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples illustrate how structural properties of P give closed-form enumerative results for e(P).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence for e(I) on J(P) (equation (3.11))
rubrics_metrics.description: If e(I) denotes number of linear extensions of the order ideal I (i.e., saturated chains from 0̂ to I in J(P)), then e(I) = Σ_{I' ⋖ I} e(I'), summing over ideals covered by I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a dynamic programming recurrence to compute e(P) by traversing J(P).
